subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Robert Fortune's Great Tea Heist
description: A micro-lesson that makes Robert Fortune's Great Tea Heist usable.

hook.text: In 1848, the British East India Company sent a botanist to steal China's tea secrets. His name was Robert Fortune.

buildup.text: Fortune disguised himself as a Chinese merchant, shaved his head, and traveled deep into restricted tea regions.

discovery.text: He smuggled out thousands of tea plants, seeds, and—critically—skilled Chinese tea workers.

twist.text: Fortune's biggest finding: black and green tea come from the same plant, processed differently.

climax.text: The stolen plants thrived in India's Darjeeling hills. Britain broke China's tea monopoly permanently.

punchline.text: One spy, some seeds, and China's monopoly was over.

quiz.question: What did Robert Fortune discover about black and green tea?
options: They come from the same plant, processed differently
Green tea is unripe black tea

details.summary: In 1848, the East India Company sent Scottish botanist Robert Fortune to China disguised in local dress to steal tea plants, seeds, and processing secrets. He succeeded, smuggling plants and skilled workers to India. This espionage broke China's tea monopoly and launched the Indian tea industry.
details.whyItMatters: Fortune's theft was one of history's most consequential acts of industrial espionage. It ended China's dominance and created India's tea empire.
takeaways: Robert Fortune disguised himself to steal tea from China in 1848
He smuggled plants, seeds, and processing knowledge to India
This broke China's monopoly and launched Indian tea production

faq.question: How did Robert Fortune smuggle tea out of China?
faq.answer: Fortune disguised himself as a Chinese merchant, traveled to restricted tea regions, collected plants and seeds, and documented processing methods. He recruited experienced Chinese tea workers to move to India. The operation took several trips over years and was backed by the East India Company.

faq.question: What was the impact of Fortune's theft on global tea trade?
faq.answer: Within decades, Indian tea plantations were producing enough to challenge Chinese exports. By the early 1900s, India and Ceylon had surpassed China as the world's leading tea exporters. The shift lasted until the late 20th century when China reclaimed the top position.
